name: Cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS, RFC1)

clinicalPearls: Late-onset, slowly progressive syndrome defined by a triad of cerebellar ataxia, sensory (ganglionopathy-type) neuropathy and bilateral vestibular failure
Caused by a biallelic AAGGG pentanucleotide repeat expansion in an intron of RFC1, inherited autosomal recessively
A longstanding dry chronic cough often precedes the neurological features by years and is a valuable diagnostic clue
Bilateral vestibular areflexia is demonstrated by an abnormal (impaired) bidirectional head-impulse test and impaired visually enhanced vestibulo-ocular reflex
The sensory neuropathy is a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy causing sensory ataxia and areflexia
Autonomic symptoms and oscillopsia on head movement are common associated features
MRI frequently shows cerebellar (especially vermian) atrophy; nerve conduction studies show a sensory neuronopathy
Management is supportive, centred on balance and vestibular rehabilitation, falls prevention and cough evaluation
reference.pathophysiology: CANVAS is caused by a biallelic AAGGG pentanucleotide repeat expansion within an intron of RFC1, which encodes the large subunit of replication factor C. The recessive expansion is thought to impair normal gene expression and RNA handling, producing a slowly progressive degeneration that converges on three vulnerable systems: the cerebellum, the dorsal root ganglia (giving a sensory neuronopathy) and the vestibular apparatus (giving bilateral vestibular failure). Involvement of sensory and autonomic ganglia and brainstem pathways also explains the frequent chronic cough and dysautonomia. The combined sensory, vestibular and cerebellar deficits summate to produce a severe multimodal balance disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Other late-onset sporadic or genetic cerebellar ataxias
Sensory neuronopathies from other causes (paraneoplastic, Sjogren syndrome, toxic, idiopathic)
Bilateral vestibulopathy from ototoxicity or other causes
Friedreich ataxia and other recessive ataxias with neuropathy
Vitamin E deficiency or other treatable sensory ataxias
additionalInvestigations: Targeted RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat-expansion analysis
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy
Vestibular function testing including the head-impulse test and caloric or video head-impulse assessment
MRI brain to document cerebellar atrophy
Screening for acquired sensory neuronopathy causes (autoimmune, paraneoplastic, Sjogren)
Assessment of chronic cough and autonomic function
redFlags: Rapidly progressive sensory neuronopathy raising concern for a paraneoplastic cause
Recurrent falls with injury from combined sensory, cerebellar and vestibular loss
Severe dysautonomia causing syncope or cardiovascular instability
Marked dysphagia in advanced disease with aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: CANVAS is slowly progressive over years to decades, with balance impairment and falls being the main sources of disability; life expectancy is usually preserved but mobility and independence decline gradually. Recognition allows targeted rehabilitation and avoidance of unnecessary investigation.
pitfalls: Investigating the ataxia, neuropathy and vestibular loss as unrelated problems and missing the unifying diagnosis
Overlooking a longstanding chronic cough that offers a strong diagnostic pointer
Failing to test the vestibulo-ocular reflex and thus missing bilateral vestibular failure
Not confirming the biallelic (recessive) nature of the RFC1 expansion, which is required for diagnosis
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
